title: TSMC and Samsung commit to ASML High-NA EUV, 12-inch photomask initiative
subtitle: The two biggest foundries outside Intel sign on to the next-generation lithography tool and to a decade-long reticle-size overhaul — both driven by AI-chip demand that current tooling cannot meet.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: TSMC and Samsung committed on September 8, 2026, to deploy ASML's High-NA extreme ultraviolet lithography machines in advanced-node production. Samsung is targeting DRAM manufacturing by 2028; TSMC is planning high-volume logic deployment starting in 2030. The two foundries become ASML's second and third High-NA customers after Intel. Each machine is priced at approximately $400 million. The same day, both companies joined ASML in a separate industry initiative to move photomasks — the patterned stencils used to transfer circuit designs onto silicon — from the current 6-inch standard to a 12-inch format, targeting 2033.

Why it matters: leading-edge chip production is the physical bottleneck under the entire AI capex build-out. High-NA EUV pushes the printable feature size down by roughly 40% versus the current EUV generation and eliminates the multi-patterning steps that currently slow yield at 2-nanometer and below. The 12-inch photomask initiative is longer-horizon but structurally larger — bigger reticles mean fewer 'stitching' constraints, larger die sizes without yield penalties, and lower cost per finished wafer once the ecosystem retools. Both are direct responses to AI-chip demand that the existing supply chain cannot meet at the price points customers want.

Context: TSMC raised its 2026 capex projection to $60–64 billion at July results, with N3 sold out and N2 already oversubscribed by Nvidia, Apple, AMD, and Broadcom. Samsung has been trying to close the foundry gap with TSMC for three years and sees the High-NA commitment as its clearest path to parity at the leading edge. ASML, meanwhile, gets its most expensive tool locked into three of the four foundries that matter, with Rapidus in Japan as the likely fourth. The industry has effectively committed a decade of capex to one lithography roadmap.

Takeaway for learners: the AI hardware stack does not start at Nvidia. Every training and inference run traces back to a few thousand square meters of cleanroom in Hsinchu, Pyeongtaek, and Chandler, and to a lithography monopoly in Veldhoven. If you are a student or early-career engineer trying to understand where AI actually gets made, spending an afternoon on how EUV works — and why High-NA is the next step — pays off more than another week of prompt-engineering practice. The physics is where the ceiling is.
